claims.text: The proposed method integrates DFT-based phonon dynamics with temperature-dependent molecular-dynamics simulations.
The hybrid method will provide accurate, decoupled predictions of lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The hybrid method will outperform Debye-temperature-based and constant-force-constant methods.
Defect-free bulk HfNbTaTiZr with minimal oxygen contamination is typical of laboratory synthesis.
DFT captures mass-disorder and force-constant-disorder effects relevant to HfNbTaTiZr.
Temperature-dependent MD captures anharmonic phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Between 300 K and 1200 K, lattice heat transport is the dominant transport contribution in the targeted samples.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Local chemical short-range order and force-constant disorder modulate phonon scattering rates and lifetimes.
First-principles DFT directly computes the phonon dispersions and scattering rates required by the proposed model.
Combining DFT and MD isolates lattice heat transport without conflating it with electronic heat transport.
The integrated method overcomes limitations caused by Debye approximations and assumptions of perfect crystals.
The model will reduce lattice-conductivity prediction error by at least 30% relative to previous approaches.
Increasing temperature enhances anharmonic phonon scattering and thereby reduces lattice thermal conductivity.
The model will clearly delineate lattice and electronic transport contributions, particularly above 300 K.
Earlier models use simple Debye-temperature estimates and ideal, defect-free crystals without accounting for local chemical fluctuations.
The proposed method is most applicable to high-purity, defect-minimized HfNbTaTiZr over the specified temperature range.
Significant defects or oxygen impurities will reduce the method's predictive accuracy.
Experimental data separating lattice and electronic conduction in HfNbTaTiZr are limited, especially at low temperatures.
Inelastic neutron scattering or time-domain thermoreflectance can independently quantify the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution for the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The method is said to overcome the limitation of assuming perfect crystals, yet its initial state and applicability boundary are themselves restricted to defect-free or defect-minimized material.
Low-temperature benchmarking below 200 K is invoked as validation of component separation, but the specified experiment only measures from 300 K to 1200 K.

The mechanism computes and isolates only lattice transport, whereas the outcome claims that the method will delineate both lattice and electronic contributions without specifying an electronic-transport calculation.
